title: Generalized Fourier's law in mesoscopic systems
abstract: Fourier's law fails when the mean free path of the energy carriers becomes comparable to the length and time scales over which the temperature field varies. We derive a thermodynamically consistent generalization in which the conductivity is promoted to a nonlocal memory operator $\bmκ_{\mathrm{eff}}(\mathbf{k},ω)$, obtained by combining mesoscopic nonequilibrium thermodynamics with the Mori--Kubo--Zwanzig projection-operator formalism. The Onsager kernel decomposes exactly into a tensor sum over vibrational normal modes weighted by their Bose heat capacities and relaxation functions, and satisfies the second law by construction. Two consequences follow. First, because the modal weights carry the directional group velocity, the kernel is anisotropic, so a nominally isotropic crystal exhibits direction-dependent apparent conductivities $Λ_z\neqΛ_r$. Second, in a pump--probe experiment the modulation frequency does not introduce temporal memory but sets the probed wavevector through the thermal penetration depth, so the suppression of the apparent conductivity measured by time-domain thermoreflectance on Si, Ge and Si$_{1-x}$Ge$_x$ is a spatial-nonlocality effect set by a sub-micron carrier mean free path. Fitting the data of Wilson and Cahill yields nonlocality lengths of $0.25$--$0.4~μ$m consistent with the mean-free-path spectra of these crystals. The framework supplies a thermodynamic foundation for the two-channel ballistic/diffusive picture of nondiffusive heat transport.
summary: This work generalizes Fourier's law by deriving a nonlocal conductivity kernel using advanced statistical mechanics techniques. It shows that heat transport in mesoscopic materials exhibits spatial nonlocality, leading to measurable apparent anisotropy even when the material itself is isotropic. The framework successfully models experimental data from TDTR measurements on semiconductors.
main_problem: Fourier's law fails when energy carrier mean free paths are comparable to system length/time scales, necessitating a thermodynamically consistent generalization for heat transport in mesoscopic systems.
main_result:
The generalized conductivity is derived as a nonlocal memory operator $\kappa_{	ext{eff}}(\mathbf{k}, \omega)$, which predicts apparent anisotropy ($\Lambda_z 
eq \Lambda_r$) even in isotropic materials due to measurement geometry.
method: The authors combine Mesoscopic Nonequilibrium Thermodynamics with the Mori–Kubo–Zwanzig projection-operator formalism to derive the nonlocal constitutive relation.
model_or_system: The theory applies to heat conduction in mesoscopic systems (like Si/SiGe) involving energy carriers (phonons, electrons), modeling the transport using a generalized Fourier law incorporating memory and spatial nonlocality.
key_observables: Apparent conductivities ($\Lambda_z$, $\Lambda_r$) measured via Time-Domain Thermoreflectance (TDTR); the nonlocal conductivity tensor $\kappa_{	ext{eff}}(\mathbf{k}, \omega)$.
important_parameters: Nonlocality length scale ($\ell$), mean free path ($\ell_c$), and frequency/wavevector dependence ($k, \omega$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on linear response theory, the assumption of small deviations from equilibrium, and approximations like the minimal one-length ansatz for $\kappa_{	ext{eff}}(k)$.
figures_summary:
Figures illustrate how a single nonlocal kernel leads to apparent anisotropy ($\Lambda_z 
eq \Lambda_r$) and show theoretical fits comparing the predicted frequency roll-off of apparent conductivity against experimental TDTR data.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from identifying the failure of Fourier's law, deriving the generalized nonlocal constitutive relation using projection operators, analyzing its consequences (anisotropy), and finally fitting these predictions to experimental measurements on semiconductor alloys.
why_interesting: While focused on thermal transport, the use of projection-operator formalism and memory kernels ($\kappa_{	ext{eff}}(\mathbf{k}, \omega)$) provides a rigorous theoretical framework for non-Markovian dynamics in open quantum systems, which is highly relevant to AMO physics.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Anisotropy from a single nonlocal kernel. The effective conductivity falls with the probed wavevector, κeff(k)/κbulk = [1 + (kℓ)2]−1. A TDTR experiment samples the through-plane direction at kz ∼d−1 p (f) and the in-plane direction at kr ∼w−1 0 , so a nominally isotropic crystal yields Λz ̸= Λr. Increasing the modulation frequency f (decreasing the spot size w0) shifts kz (kr) outward, selectively suppress- ing each channel.

FIG. 2. Apparent thermal conductivity ΛA versus modula- tion frequency: the spatial-nonlocality model, Eq. (11) (solid lines), against TDTR data of Wilson and Cahill [10] (symbols, with error bars; digitized from their Fig. 3a at w0 = 10 µm). Fourier’s law predicts a constant ΛA; Si and Si:B stay flat while Ge and the SiGe alloys are suppressed at high f, where the shrinking penetration depth dp(f) probes a larger wavevector. Solid lines are two-parameter fits of Eq. (11); the resolved nonlocality lengths are ℓ= 0.41, 0.34 and 0.25 µm for Ge, Si0.99Ge0.01 and Si0.2Ge0.8, respectively.
